title: Alberta Society Search: Look Up Any Non-Profit Free
h1: Alberta Society Search: Look Up Any of 70,000+ Registered Non-Profits
description: Search all 70,000+ Alberta societies and non-profits by name, free — current status from Alberta's official monthly listing. Is your society active?
body:
**Looking for an Alberta society or non-profit?** Search it by name at the top of this page — all 70,000+ organizations on Alberta's official non-profit listing, free, with current status.

Alberta has more than 70,000 registered non-profit organizations — societies, religious societies, agricultural societies and non-profit companies — and you can search all of them by name in the lookup above, free. The data comes from Alberta's official monthly non-profit listing (the same dataset behind the province's [Non-profit Listing Dashboard](https://www.alberta.ca/alberta-non-profit-listing-dashboard)), refreshed every month, so the status you see — Active, Struck, Dissolved — is the registry's own. This matters more than most people expect: most society lookups fail elsewhere, because societies don't appear in the federal registry index that ordinary corporation searches rely on. Here's what the search covers, what each status means, and what to do with what you find.

## Why don't Alberta societies show up in normal corporation searches?

Because the usual search tools index *business corporations*, not societies. Canada's Business Registries — the federal index behind most "search a company" tools — carries Alberta corporations registered under the Business Corporations Act, but organizations incorporated under Alberta's *Societies Act*, the Religious Societies' Land Act, or Part 9 of the Companies Act (non-profit companies) simply aren't in it. Search a legitimate, decades-old community society in a standard corporate search and you'll get "no results" — which reads, wrongly, as "this organization doesn't exist."

The province publishes the real list: a monthly export of every registered non-profit, with its legal type, status, registration date and location. That's the dataset this page searches. As of the current listing it breaks down to roughly 55,000 Alberta Societies, 4,200 religious societies, 5,200 non-profit private companies, 3,800 extra-provincial non-profits registered in Alberta, plus agricultural societies, recreation companies and private-act corporations.

## How do you search for an Alberta society?

Type the society's name — or the distinctive part of it — into the search at the top of this page and pick it from the results. Each result shows the organization's legal type, its registry status, its registration date and its city. A few tips for names that don't surface on the first try:

1. **Use the legal name, not the working name.** Many groups operate as "Riverbend Community League" while the registered name is "RIVERBEND COMMUNITY LEAGUE SOCIETY". Try the core words first; the search matches from the start of the name and across words.
2. **Drop punctuation and abbreviations.** "St. Albert" may be registered as "ST ALBERT"; "Assn" as "ASSOCIATION".
3. **Check the type.** A church may be a Religious Society rather than an Alberta Society; a community rink may be an Agricultural Society or a Recreation Company. The type shown on each result tells you which law the organization lives under.

Searching a business corporation instead? Use the [Canada-wide corporation search](/canada-corporations-search) — and for Alberta corporations specifically, our [Alberta annual return guide](/articles/how-to-file-your-annual-return-in-alberta) explains the filings that keep them in good standing.

## What does the society's status mean?

The listing uses the registry's own status values. The three you'll see most:

- **Active** — the society exists and is in good standing with Corporate Registry. About 28,500 organizations on the current listing are Active.
- **Struck** — the Registrar removed the society from the register, almost always for not filing its annual returns. A struck society has ceased to exist as a legal entity: it can't legally contract, hold property in its name or receive grants. The current listing carries over 36,000 struck organizations — more than are active, which says a lot about how quietly annual-return defaults accumulate.
- **Dissolved** — the society was wound up, either voluntarily or following a strike.

You may also see transitional states like Start (newly registered), Amalgamated, or Pending Revival/Restoration. If your own society shows Struck and that's news to you, the registry's reminders were probably going to a stale address — the fix starts with bringing the filings current and, where the strike has already happened, applying for revival through Corporate Registry.

## How do Alberta societies stay in good standing?

By filing the society annual return every year. It's a different filing from the corporate annual return: societies file **form REG3185 directly with Alberta Corporate Registry** — by mail or email, with financial statements and the current list of directors attached — not through an authorized registry agent the way corporations file. The deadline is the last day of the month following the society's anniversary month. Our [Alberta society annual return guide](/articles/alberta-society-annual-return) walks through the form, the attachments and the deadline in full, and what happens when filings lapse (the Struck column above is what happens).

One caution worth repeating from that guide: because the registry's reminder goes to the society's registered address, and volunteer boards turn over, the most common path to being struck is simply never seeing the reminders. If the search shows your society Active, check the registration date against your records and confirm someone currently on the board owns the annual filing.

## How do you verify a non-profit before donating or partnering?

Three checks, in order:

1. **Confirm it exists and is Active** — the search above, thirty seconds, free. A grant application, donation drive or venue contract in the name of a Struck society is a real and surprisingly common problem.
2. **Pull the registry record if money is involved.** For formal due diligence — funding agreements, property transactions, litigation — order the organization's registry documents. We retrieve official Alberta registry records for {{price:profile-report}} + tax, [ordered from the search result](/canada-corporations-search) or [by asking us directly](/contact).
3. **Check charitable status separately if tax receipts matter.** "Registered society" and "registered charity" are different things: the first is Alberta corporate law, the second is CRA registration. A society that isn't a registered charity can't issue donation tax receipts — look the organization up in the CRA's charities listing for that half of the picture, and see our guide to [verifying a Canadian company](/guides/how-to-verify-a-canadian-company) for the general method.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I find out if an Alberta society is still active?

Search its name at the top of this page. The result shows the registry's current status — Active, Struck or Dissolved — from Alberta's official monthly non-profit listing. Active means it exists and is in good standing; Struck means it has been removed from the register, usually for unfiled annual returns.

### Why can't I find a society in other corporation searches?

Most corporation searches query the federal registry index, which only carries Alberta's business corporations. Societies, religious societies and Part 9 non-profit companies are registered under different Alberta statutes and never appear there. This page searches the province's own non-profit listing instead, which is the complete register.

### How many non-profits are registered in Alberta?

The official listing currently carries over 70,000 organizations: roughly 55,000 Alberta Societies, with the rest religious societies, agricultural societies, non-profit private and public companies, recreation companies and extra-provincial non-profits. About 28,500 are Active — tens of thousands of the rest are Struck, mostly over unfiled annual returns.

### What should a society do if it has been struck?

A struck society has lost its legal existence, so act before signing anything in its name: bring the outstanding annual returns and attachments together and apply to Alberta Corporate Registry for revival. If the strike is recent, start with the registry's requirements for reinstatement — and fix the registered address that let the reminders go missing. [Contact us](/contact) if you need the organization's registry records to see exactly where things stand.
